cues.text: Final consolidation.
This is the chapter where we pull together everything from this study session and ask one question: what separates genuine digital transformation from simply buying technology?
Let us begin with the goal of this chapter.
You are expected to understand a set of ideas, and I will name them in the order the material gives them, so you can use them as a checklist.
First, the AI capability categories.
These describe what kinds of things artificial intelligence systems can do, and how broad or narrow that ability is.
Keep in mind that a capability category tells you what a system is able to do, not whether doing it will help your organisation.
Second, machine learning and deep learning, together with the learning types.
Machine learning, often shortened to ML, is the approach where a system learns patterns from data instead of following only rules that a person wrote out by hand.
Deep learning, or DL, is a more specialised branch of machine learning that uses layered neural networks.
The learning types then describe how that learning takes place, for example whether the data comes with correct answers attached or not.
As you review, make sure you can say clearly how ML and DL relate, and how each learning type differs from the others.
Third, automation choices.
Here the question is not simply whether to automate, but which form of automation suits a given task, and what that choice means for cost, control and risk.
Whenever you meet a scenario, ask what is being automated, why, and what the alternatives were.
Fourth, the five Vs.
These are the five characteristics used to describe big data.
They help you judge whether data is large, fast, varied, trustworthy and valuable enough to support the decisions an organisation wants to make.
Be ready to name all five and explain each one in plain language.
Fifth, data architecture.
This is the structure that governs how data is collected, stored, organised, moved and made available for use.
Without a sound architecture, even excellent data cannot reach the people and systems that need it.
Sixth, the four analytics categories.
These describe progressively more demanding questions an organisation can ask of its data, from understanding what has already happened, through to deciding what action to take.
You should be able to place any business question into the right category.
Seventh, the components of business intelligence, or BI.
Business intelligence is the set of tools and practices that turn raw data into information managers can act on.
Know the parts that make up a BI capability and how they connect, from data sources through to the reports and dashboards decision makers see.
Eighth, ethical safeguards.
These are the protections that keep data and AI use fair, transparent, accountable and respectful of people.
Technology that works technically but harms or misleads people is not a success, so safeguards belong in the design from the start and not as an afterthought.
Now the second sentence of the block, which carries the key lesson of the whole chapter.
It tells you to use business outcomes and validated evidence to distinguish useful transformation from technology adoption.
Let us unpack that carefully, because it connects back to the distinction you met at the start of the course.
Technology adoption means acquiring and installing a tool: a new platform, a machine learning model, an automation, a dashboard.
Digital transformation is different.
It is a change in how the organisation creates value, and that change shows up in results the business actually cares about.
So the test has two parts.
The first is business outcomes.
Ask what changed for the organisation or its customers.
Did a process become faster, cheaper or more reliable?
Did a decision improve?
Did the customer experience get better?
If you cannot point to an outcome like that, you may only have adopted a technology.
The second part is validated evidence.
A claim that something worked is not enough.
Validated means the result has been checked, for example against measured data, tests or independent review, rather than accepted because a vendor, a team or an enthusiastic report said so.
This links directly to the safeguards we just listed.
Evidence should be honest about its limits, and where the evidence is incomplete, you should say so instead of guessing.
Put simply, when you face any case or exam scenario, move through three steps.
Identify the technology involved and which capability, learning type, data or analytics concept it reflects.
Then ask which business outcome it was meant to deliver.
Finally, ask what validated evidence shows that the outcome was achieved, and whether ethical safeguards were in place.
If the outcome and the evidence are present, you are looking at useful transformation.
If only the technology is present, you are looking at adoption.
Carry that test with you into every case you study, and use the eight topics above as your checklist for revision.
